steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the section of an encyclopedia article on the ALGOL 68-R compiler that explains which restrictions it placed on the ALGOL 68 language so it could compile in one pass, with a subsection and short code examples for each restriction.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Overview: the subset ALGOL 68-R implemented, and the revised report
### Specification before use
### No proceduring
### Explicit void mode
### No formal declarers
### No parallel processing
### goto may not be omitted
### Uniting is only allowed in strong positions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Overview
  - one pass compiling -> subset of language from original report
  - list: specify identifiers/modes/operators before use; no automatic proceduring; explicit VOID mode; no formal declarers; no parallel processing; GOTO not omittable; uniting only in strong positions
  - many adopted by revised report
### Specification before use
- all identifiers declared before use
- [code: even/odd mutual recursion, standard version and rewritten version with PROC (INT) BOOL odd;]
- recursive mode declarations: stub mode declaration tells compiler up-coming symbol is a mode not operator
- [code: MODE B; stub example]
### No proceduring
- proceduring coercion (strong context): expression -> procedure returning its type; used for call by name
- also in procedure declarations: [code: PROC x plus 1 = INT : x + 1;] RHS = cast, then converted to procedure
- 68-R team: too hard; two changes: coercion dropped; mode : expression = procedure denotation; casts use explicit VAL
- [code: REAL : x vs REAL VAL x]
- call by name (e.g. Jensen's device) -> pass procedure denotation [code: PROC sum example]
- revised report accepted these; cast form changed to mode (expression) [code: REAL (x)]
### Explicit void mode
- original: VOID = empty mode [code examples]
- 68-R: explicit VOID symbol, simpler parsing, more readable [code examples]
- adopted by revised report
### No formal declarers
- formal declarers = modes on LHS of identity declaration / in procedure declaration
- original: could include bounds, and fixed / FLEX / EITHER [code examples]
- 68-R: formal = virtual declarers, no bounds; fewer parsing ambiguities; not needed in working programs
- procedures check bounds themselves with UPB, LWB
- [code: recoded example, bounds from caller]
- revised report: formal bounds also removed, FLEX moved so it can be in formal declarers [code comparison]
### No parallel processing
- ALGOL 68: PAR + collateral clause [code: producer, consumer]
- semaphore type SEMA, P (DOWN) and V (UP)
- not in 68-R
- extension ALGOL 68-RT: ICL 1900 subprogramming feature -> multithreading, like modern thread libraries
  - compiler unchanged; only runtime library and linker
### goto may not be omitted
- ALGOL 68: GOTO could be omitted [code: stop example]
- one pass compiler -> too difficult -> GOTO obligatory
- same restriction in official sublanguage ALGOL 68S
### Uniting is only allowed in strong positions
- uniting: coercion producing UNION from constituent mode [code: IBOOL]
- standard: firm or strong contexts, e.g. operands of formulas [code: ISTRUE]
- 68-R: too many ambiguities -> strong contexts only
- effects rarely important; work around with a cast for strong context

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
ALGOL 68-R implemented a subset of the language that was defined in the original report, so that it could compile in one pass:

Identifiers, modes and operators must be specified before use.

No automatic proceduring

Explicit VOID mode

No formal declarers

No parallel processing

GOTO may not be omitted

Uniting is only valid in strong positions

The revised report on ALGOL 68 adopted many of these restrictions.

### Specification before use

ALGOL 68-R insisted that all identifiers had to be specified (declared) before they were used, so that compiling could be done in one pass.

So the standard program:

PROC even = (INT number) BOOL: ( number = 0 | TRUE | odd (ABS (number - 1)));

PROC odd = (INT number) BOOL: ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

would need to be rewritten like this:

PROC (INT) BOOL odd;

PROC even = (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | TRUE | odd (ABS (number - 1)));

odd := (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

For recursive declarations of modes (types), a special stub mode declaration was used. It told the compiler that a symbol that was coming up was a mode and not an operator:

MODE B;

MODE A = STRUCT (REF B b);

MODE B = [1:10] REF A;

### No proceduring

In the standard language, the proceduring coercion could convert an expression of some type into a procedure that returns that type, in a strong context. It could be used to implement call by name.

Proceduring was also used in another case, which was the declaration of procedures. In the declaration:

PROC x plus 1 = INT : x + 1;

the right hand side was a cast of x + 1 to integer, and then this was converted to a procedure returning integer.

The ALGOL 68-R team found this too difficult to handle, so they made two changes to the language. They dropped the proceduring coercion, and they redefined the form mode : expression as a procedure denotation, and casts were indicated by an explicit VAL symbol:

REAL : x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68 CO

REAL VAL x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68-R CO

If code had a valid use for call by name (for example Jensen's device) it could just pass a procedure denotation:

PROC sum = (INT lo, hi, PROC (INT) REAL term) REAL :

BEGIN

REAL temp := 0;

FOR i FROM lo TO hi DO

temp +:= term (i);

temp

END;

print (sum (1, 100, (INT i) REAL: 1/i))

These changes were accepted in the version of the language that was defined in the revised report, but the form of the cast was changed slightly to mode (expression).

REAL (x) CO a cast to REAL in revised ALGOL 68 CO

### Explicit void mode

The original language represented the VOID mode by an empty mode:

: x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

The ALGOL 68-R team decided to use an explicit VOID symbol to make parsing simpler (and to make it more readable):

VOID VAL x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = VOID : GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

The ALGOL 68 revised report adopted this modification of the language.

### No formal declarers
- formal declarers = modes on LHS of identity declaration or in procedure declaration; original could include bounds and fixed/FLEX/EITHER

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [ 3 : ] INT b = a; CO This is an error CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1 : EITHER] INT a) : ...

- 68-R: formal = virtual declarers, no bounds; fewer parsing ambiguities; not used in working programs
- check bounds with UPB (upper bound) and LWB (lower bound)
- recoded example (bounds from caller):

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [] INT b = a [ AT 3]; CO use slice so b has bounds 3:17 CO

PROC x = (REF [] INT a) VOID: ... CO bounds given by caller CO

- revised report: formal bounds removed too, FLEX moved into formal declarers:

[ 1: FLEX ] INT a; CO original ALGOL 68, or ALGOL 68-R CO

FLEX [ 1: ] INT a; CO revised ALGOL 68, CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1: FLEX ] INT a) : ... CO Original ALGOL 68 CO

PROC x = (REF [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO ALGOL 68-R CO

PROC x = (REF FLEX [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO Revised ALGOL 68 CO

### No parallel processing
- PAR + collateral clause:

PAR BEGIN

producer,

consumer

END

- SEMA with P (DOWN) and V (UP); not in 68-R
- ALGOL 68-RT extension: ICL 1900 subprogramming -> multithreading like modern thread libraries; only runtime library and linker changed

### goto may not be omitted
- GOTO could be omitted:

PROC stop = : ...;

BEGIN

IF x > 3 THEN stop FI; CO a jump, not a call CO

stop:

SKIP

END

- one pass compiler -> too difficult -> GOTO obligatory; same in ALGOL 68S

### Uniting is only allowed in strong positions
- uniting = coercion producing a UNION from a constituent mode:

MODE IBOOL = UNION (INT, BOOL); CO an IBOOL is an INT or a BOOL CO

IBOOL a = TRUE; CO the BOOL value TRUE is united to an IBOOL CO

- standard: firm or strong contexts, e.g. operands of formulas:

OP ISTRUE = (IBOOL a) BOOL: ...;

IF ISTRUE 1 CO legal because 1 (INT) can be united to IBOOL CO

THEN ...

- 68-R: too many ambiguities -> strong contexts only; rarely important, workaround with a cast

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
ALGOL 68-R implemented a subset of the language that was defined in the original report, so that it could compile in one pass:

Identifiers, modes and operators must be specified before use.

No automatic proceduring

Explicit VOID mode

No formal declarers

No parallel processing

GOTO may not be omitted

Uniting is only valid in strong positions

The revised report on ALGOL 68 adopted many of these restrictions.

### Specification before use

ALGOL 68-R insisted that all identifiers had to be specified (declared) before they were used, so that compiling could be done in one pass.

So the standard program:

PROC odd = (INT number) BOOL: ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

would need to be rewritten like this:

PROC even = (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | TRUE | odd (ABS (number - 1)));

odd := (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

For recursive declarations of modes (types), a special stub mode declaration was used. It told the compiler that a symbol that was coming up was a mode and not an operator:

MODE B;

MODE A = STRUCT (REF B b);

MODE B = [1:10] REF A;

### No proceduring

In the standard language, the proceduring coercion could convert an expression of some type into a procedure that returns that type, in a strong context. It could be used to implement call by name.

Proceduring was also used in another case, which was the declaration of procedures. In the declaration:

PROC x plus 1 = INT : x + 1;

the right hand side was a cast of x + 1 to integer, and then this was converted to a procedure returning integer.

The ALGOL 68-R team found this too difficult to handle, so they made two changes to the language. They dropped the proceduring coercion, and they redefined the form mode : expression as a procedure denotation, and casts were indicated by an explicit VAL symbol:

REAL : x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68 CO

REAL VAL x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68-R CO

If code had a valid use for call by name (for example Jensen's device) it could just pass a procedure denotation:

PROC sum = (INT lo, hi, PROC (INT) REAL term) REAL :

BEGIN

REAL temp := 0;

FOR i FROM lo TO hi DO

temp +:= term (i);

temp

END;

print (sum (1, 100, (INT i) REAL: 1/i))

These changes were accepted in the version of the language that was defined in the revised report, but the form of the cast was changed slightly to mode (expression).

REAL (x) CO a cast to REAL in revised ALGOL 68 CO

### Explicit void mode

The original language represented the VOID mode by an empty mode:

: x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

The ALGOL 68-R team decided to use an explicit VOID symbol to make parsing simpler (and to make it more readable):

VOID VAL x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = VOID : GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

The ALGOL 68 revised report adopted this modification of the language.

### No formal declarers

Formal declarers are the modes on the left hand side of an identity declaration, or the modes that are specified in a procedure declaration. In the original language they could include array bounds, and they specified if the matching actual declarer was fixed, FLEX or EITHER:

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [ 3 : ] INT b = a; CO This is an error CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1 : EITHER] INT a) : ...

The ALGOL 68-R team redefined formal declarers so they were the same as virtual declarers, which do not include bound information. They found that this reduced the ambiguities when parsing the language, and they felt it was not a feature that working programs would use.

A procedure that needed certain bounds for its arguments could check them itself using the UPB (upper bound) and LWB (lower bound) operators.

The example above could be recoded like this in ALGOL 68-R (the bounds of a in the procedure would depend on the caller):

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [] INT b = a [ AT 3]; CO use slice so b has bounds 3:17 CO

PROC x = (REF [] INT a) VOID: ... CO bounds given by caller CO

The revised report on ALGOL 68 also removed formal bounds, but it moved the position of the FLEX indication so that it could be included in formal declarers:

[ 1: FLEX ] INT a; CO original ALGOL 68, or ALGOL 68-R CO

FLEX [ 1: ] INT a; CO revised ALGOL 68, CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1: FLEX ] INT a) : ... CO Original ALGOL 68 CO

PROC x = (REF [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO ALGOL 68-R CO

PROC x = (REF FLEX [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO Revised ALGOL 68 CO

### No parallel processing

In ALGOL 68 code can be run in parallel by writing PAR and then a collateral clause, for example in:

PAR BEGIN

producer,

consumer

END

the procedures producer and consumer will run in parallel. A semaphore type (SEMA) is provided with the traditional P (DOWN) and V (UP) operators for synchronizing between the parts of the parallel clause.

ALGOL 68-R did not implement this feature.

An extension called ALGOL 68-RT was written, which used the subprogramming feature of the ICL 1900 to give ALGOL 68-R programs multithreading facilities, with semantics similar to modern thread libraries. There were no changes to the compiler, only to the runtime library and the linker.

### goto may not be omitted

In ALGOL 68 the GOTO symbol could be left out of a jump:

PROC stop = : ...;

BEGIN

IF x > 3 THEN stop FI; CO a jump, not a call CO

stop:

SKIP

END

Since ALGOL 68-R was a one pass compiler this was too difficult, and so the GOTO symbol was made obligatory.

The official sublanguage, ALGOL 68S, made the same restriction.

### Uniting is only allowed in strong positions

In ALGOL 68, uniting is the coercion that produces a UNION from a constituent mode, for example:

MODE IBOOL = UNION (INT, BOOL); CO an IBOOL is an INT or a BOOL CO

IBOOL a = TRUE; CO the BOOL value TRUE is united to an IBOOL CO

In standard ALGOL 68 uniting was possible in firm or strong contexts, so for example it could be applied to the operands of formulas:

OP ISTRUE = (IBOOL a) BOOL: ...;

IF ISTRUE 1 CO legal because 1 (INT) can be united to IBOOL CO

THEN ...

The ALGOL 68-R implementers found that this gave too many ambiguous situations, so they restricted the uniting coercion to strong contexts.

The effects of this restriction were rarely important, and if necessary they could be worked around by using a cast to give a strong context at the point in the program where it was needed.

steps.text:
To allow one pass compiling, ALGOL 68-R implemented a subset of the language defined in the original report:[1]

Identifiers, modes and operators must be specified before use.

No automatic proceduring

Explicit VOID mode

No formal declarers

No parallel processing

GOTO may not be omitted

Uniting is only valid in strong positions

Many of these restrictions were adopted by the revised report on ALGOL 68.

### Specification before use

To allow compiling in one pass, ALGOL 68-R insisted that all identifiers be specified (declared) before use.

The standard program:

PROC even = (INT number) BOOL: ( number = 0 | TRUE | odd (ABS (number - 1)));

PROC odd = (INT number) BOOL: ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

would have to be rewritten as:

PROC (INT) BOOL odd;

PROC even = (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | TRUE | odd (ABS (number - 1)));

odd := (INT number) BOOL : ( number = 0 | FALSE | even (ABS (number - 1)));

To allow recursive declarations of modes (types), a special stub mode declaration was used to tell the compiler that an up-coming symbol was a mode rather than an operator:

MODE B;

MODE A = STRUCT (REF B b);

MODE B = [1:10] REF A;

### No proceduring

In the standard language, the proceduring coercion could, in a strong context, convert an expression of some type into a procedure returning that type. This could be used to implement call by name.

Proceduring was also used in the declaration of procedures. In the declaration:

PROC x plus 1 = INT : x + 1;

the right hand side was a cast of x + 1 to integer, which was then converted to a procedure returning integer.

The ALGOL 68-R team found this too difficult to handle and made two changes to the language. The proceduring coercion was dropped, and the form mode : expression was redefined as a procedure denotation, with casts indicated by an explicit VAL symbol:

REAL : x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68 CO

REAL VAL x CO a cast to REAL in ALGOL 68-R CO

Code that had a valid use for call by name (for example, Jensen's device) could simply pass a procedure denotation:

PROC sum = (INT lo, hi, PROC (INT) REAL term) REAL :

BEGIN

REAL temp := 0;

FOR i FROM lo TO hi DO

temp +:= term (i);

temp

END;

print (sum (1, 100, (INT i) REAL: 1/i))

These changes were accepted in the version of the language defined in the revised report, although the form of the cast was slightly changed to mode (expression).

REAL (x) CO a cast to REAL in revised ALGOL 68 CO

### Explicit void mode

In the original language the VOID mode was represented by an empty mode:

: x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

The ALGOL 68-R team decided to use an explicit VOID symbol to simplify parsing (and increase readability):

VOID VAL x := 3.14; CO cast (x := 3.14) to void CO

PROC endit = VOID : GOTO end; CO a procedure returning void CO

This modification was adopted by the ALGOL 68 revised report.

### No formal declarers

Formal declarers are the modes on the left hand side of an identity declaration, or the modes specified in a procedure declaration. In the original language they could include array bounds, and they specified whether the matching actual declarer was fixed, FLEX or EITHER:

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [ 3 : ] INT b = a; CO This is an error CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1 : EITHER] INT a) : ...

The ALGOL 68-R team redefined formal declarers to be the same as virtual declarers, which include no bound information. They found that this reduced ambiguities in parsing the language, and felt that it was not a feature that would be used in working programs.

If a procedure needed certain bounds for its arguments, it could check them itself with the UPB (upper bound) and LWB (lower bound) operators.

In ALGOL 68-R the example above could be recoded like this (the bounds of a in the procedure would depend on the caller):

[ 15 ] INT a; CO an actual declarer, bounds 1:15 CO

REF [] INT b = a [ AT 3]; CO use slice so b has bounds 3:17 CO

PROC x = (REF [] INT a) VOID: ... CO bounds given by caller CO

In the revised report on ALGOL 68 formal bounds were also removed, but the FLEX indication was moved so that it could be included in formal declarers:

[ 1: FLEX ] INT a; CO original ALGOL 68, or ALGOL 68-R CO

FLEX [ 1: ] INT a; CO revised ALGOL 68, CO

PROC x = (REF [ 1: FLEX ] INT a) : ... CO Original ALGOL 68 CO

PROC x = (REF [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO ALGOL 68-R CO

PROC x = (REF FLEX [ ] INT a) VOID: ... CO Revised ALGOL 68 CO

### No parallel processing

In ALGOL 68 code can be run in parallel by writing PAR followed by a collateral clause, for example in:

PAR BEGIN

producer,

consumer

END

the procedures producer and consumer will be run in parallel. A semaphore type (SEMA) with the traditional P (DOWN) and V (UP) operators is provided for synchronizing between the parts of the parallel clause.

This feature was not implemented in ALGOL 68-R.

An extension named ALGOL 68-RT was written that used the subprogramming feature of the ICL 1900 to provide multithreading facilities to ALGOL 68-R programs, with semantics similar to modern thread libraries.[2] No changes were made to the compiler, only to the runtime library and the linker.

### goto may not be omitted

In ALGOL 68 the GOTO symbol could be omitted from a jump:

PROC stop = : ...;

BEGIN

IF x > 3 THEN stop FI; CO a jump, not a call CO

stop:

SKIP

END

As ALGOL 68-R was a one pass compiler this was too difficult, so the GOTO symbol was made obligatory.

The same restriction was made in the official sublanguage, ALGOL 68S.[3]

### Uniting is only allowed in strong positions

In ALGOL 68, uniting is the coercion that produces a UNION from a constituent mode, for example:

MODE IBOOL = UNION (INT, BOOL); CO an IBOOL is an INT or a BOOL CO

IBOOL a = TRUE; CO the BOOL value TRUE is united to an IBOOL CO

In standard ALGOL 68 uniting was possible in firm or strong contexts, so it could for example be applied to the operands of formulas:

OP ISTRUE = (IBOOL a) BOOL: ...;

IF ISTRUE 1 CO legal because 1 (INT) can be united to IBOOL CO

THEN ...

The ALGOL 68-R implementers found this gave too many ambiguous situations, so they restricted the uniting coercion to strong contexts.

The effects of this restriction were rarely important and, if necessary, could be worked around by using a cast to provide a strong context at the required point in the program.
